name: Memphis Design style

lead: Memphis Design comes from the Memphis Group, founded in Milan in 1980 by Ettore Sottsass. It uses saturated colours, squiggles, terrazzo and laminate patterns and asymmetrical geometric shapes, and has returned repeatedly as a fashion and graphic look.

For appearance, people borrow it through clothing, prints, accessories and bold colour-blocked outfits to create a playful, high-contrast style. It is a styling choice rather than a physical change, and has no clinical research.

paras: People wear Memphis-inspired prints, geometric earrings and bags, and colour-blocked outfits, often mixing patterns on purpose. The aesthetic also appears in hair accessories and graphic makeup.
No health risks are specific to the style. Because the look is deliberately loud, it can read as costume-like in some settings; this is a matter of taste.

lead: Memphis Design is the style of the Memphis Group, an Italian design and architecture collective founded by Ettore Sottsass on the evening of 6 December 1980 and active until 1987. Its furniture, lighting, textiles, ceramics and glass objects were colourful, abstract and asymmetrical, with frequent use of plastic laminate and terrazzo.[1]

The group took its name from a Bob Dylan record playing at its first meeting.[1] Its look spread into television, film, fashion and household goods from the mid-1980s to mid-1990s, was later succeeded by the Y2K aesthetic, and resurfaced in the 2010s through vaporwave and flat 'Corporate Memphis' illustration.[1]

In dress, designers have referenced it: Dior's autumn/winter 2011-12 haute couture show and Missoni's 2015 collection drew on Memphis designs, and former Memphis member Nathalie Du Pasquier designed patterned bags for HAY and a collection for American Apparel.[1]
infobox: Bright colours, geometric shapes, laminate, terrazzo

paras: Sottsass founded Memphis Milano in 1980 and left the group in 1985 to concentrate on his own firm; the group ended in 1987.[1] The Carlton room divider is a well-known piece, built from inexpensive plastic laminates for a luxury market.[1]

The style's colour clashes and patterns were taken up in 1980s and 1990s clothing and returned in 2010s runway collections and online aesthetics.[1] Nathalie Du Pasquier's textile and accessory work carried the patterns into wearable products.[1]
